claim: Sexual interactions have a potent influence on health in several species, including mammals.
source: Sexual interactions have a potent influence on health in several species, including mammals.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent citations in the introduction.

claim: Previous work in C. elegans identified strategies used by males to accelerate the demise of the opposite sex (hermaphrodites).
source: Previous work in C. elegans identified strategies used by males to accelerate the demise of the opposite sex (hermaphrodites).
evidence: This statement references prior research findings, which are cited later in the manuscript.

claim: Young C. elegans hermaphrodites are remarkably resistant to brief sexual encounters with males.
source: Here we discover that young C. elegans hermaphrodites are remarkably resistant to brief sexual encounters with males, whereas older hermaphrodites succumb prematurely.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1F.

claim: Older hermaphrodites succumb prematurely to brief sexual encounters with males.
source: Here we discover that young C. elegans hermaphrodites are remarkably resistant to brief sexual encounters with males, whereas older hermaphrodites succumb prematurely.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1G.

claim: It is not youthfulness that protects young hermaphrodites, but the fact that they have self-sperm.
source: Surprisingly, it is not their youthfulness that protects young hermaphrodites, but the fact that they have self-sperm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing young hermaphrodites with self-sperm to young feminized individuals without self-sperm (Figure 2).

claim: The beneficial effect of self-sperm is mediated by a sperm-sensing pathway acting on the soma rather than by fertilization.
source: The beneficial effect of self-sperm is mediated by a sperm-sensing pathway acting on the soma rather than by fertilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with fertilization-defective mutants (spe-9) shown in Figure 3E-F and experiments manipulating the CEH-18/VAB-1 pathway shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activation of the sperm-sensing pathway in females triggers protection from the negative impact of males.
source: Activation of this pathway in females triggers protection from the negative impact of males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that blocking CEH-18 and VAB-1 in feminized individuals protects them from mating-induced demise (Figure 4B-C).

claim: The role of self-sperm in protecting against the detrimental effects of males evolved independently in hermaphroditic nematodes.
source: Interestingly, the role of self-sperm in protecting against the detrimental effects of males evolved independently in hermaphroditic nematodes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in C. briggsae showing similar protection mechanisms (Figure 5C-F) and phylogenetic analysis showing independent evolution of hermaphroditism.

claim: In Drosophila and C. elegans, sexual interactions are detrimental to health and shorten the lifespan of both sexes.
source: In Drosophila and C. elegans, sexual interactions are detrimental to health and shorten the lifespan of both sexes (Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2016; Chapman et al., 1995; Fowler and Partridge, 1989; Gems and Riddle, 1996; Gendron et al., 2014; Harvanek et al., 2017; Maures et al., 2014; Partridge and Farquhar, 1981; Promislow, 2003; Promislow, 1992; Shi and Murphy, 2014; Shi et al., 2017; Ting et al., 2014; Van Voorhies, 1992; Woodruff et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals, mates induce neurological, developmental, and behavioral changes in the opposite sex and can negatively impact health.
source: In mammals, mates induce neurological, developmental, and behavioral changes in the opposite sex and can negatively impact health (Gao et al., 2017; Garratt et al., 2016; Aloise King et al., 2013; Stowers and Kuo, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The presence of males can increase female body weight.
source: For example, the presence of males can increase female body weight (Garratt et al., 2016) and accelerate puberty (Flanagan et al., 2011; Vandenbergh, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of males can accelerate puberty in females.
source: For example, the presence of males can increase female body weight (Garratt et al., 2016) and accelerate puberty (Flanagan et al., 2011; Vandenbergh, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Males shorten the lifespan of the C. elegans hermaphrodite through a phenomenon called male-induced demise.
source: Males shorten the lifespan of the C. elegans hermaphrodite through a phenomenon called male-induced demise (Gems and Riddle, 1996; Maures et al., 2014; Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Males shorten hermaphrodite lifespan by several means including sperm, seminal fluid, and pheromones.
source: Previous studies showed that males shorten hermaphrodite lifespan by several means (e.g. sperm, seminal fluid, and pheromones), and identified some of the hermaphrodite genes that mediate male-induced demise (e.g. utx-1, ins-11, daf-16) (Maures et al., 2014; Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some hermaphrodite genes that mediate male-induced demise include utx-1, ins-11, and daf-16.
source: Previous studies showed that males shorten hermaphrodite lifespan by several means (e.g. sperm, seminal fluid, and pheromones), and identified some of the hermaphrodite genes that mediate male-induced demise (e.g. utx-1, ins-11, daf-16) (Maures et al., 2014; Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long and frequent sexual interactions with young males shortened hermaphrodite lifespan.
source: As previously shown (Gems and Riddle, 1996; Maures et al., 2014; Shi and Murphy, 2014), long and frequent sexual interactions with young males shortened hermaphrodite lifespan (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: Middle-aged males were less able to induce premature demise of the opposite sex than young males.
source: Middle-aged males were less able to induce premature demise of the opposite sex than young males (Figure 1B), probably because of their decreased ability to efficiently mate (Guo et al., 2012) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 3, with a citation providing context.

claim: Middle-aged males have a decreased ability to efficiently mate compared to young males.
source: Middle-aged males were less able to induce premature demise of the opposite sex than young males (Figure 1B), probably because of their decreased ability to efficiently mate (Guo et al., 2012) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Hermaphrodites that interacted with males for 24 hr when young lived shorter than hermaphrodites that never interact with males.
source: Hermaphrodites that interacted with males for 24 hr when young from day 3 to 4 of life (C, red dashed line) or middle-aged from day 6 to 7 of life (D, orange dashed line) lived shorter than hermaphrodites that never interact with males (p=0.029 and p<0.0001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance.

claim: Hermaphrodites that interacted with males for 24 hr when middle-aged lived shorter than hermaphrodites that never interact with males.
source: Hermaphrodites that interacted with males for 24 hr when young from day 3 to 4 of life (C, red dashed line) or middle-aged from day 6 to 7 of life (D, orange dashed line) lived shorter than hermaphrodites that never interact with males (p=0.029 and p<0.0001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance.

claim: Hermaphrodites that mated within a brief (2 hr) interaction with males when young did not have a shortened lifespan.
source: Hermaphrodites that mated within a brief (2 hr) interaction with males when young on day 3 of life (C, lime green dashed line) did not have a shortened lifespan (n.s. vs. no males) but hermaphrodites that mated within a brief period (2 hr) when middle-aged on day 7 of life (D, green dashed line) did have a significantly shortened lifespan (p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Hermaphrodites that mated within a brief (2 hr) interaction with males when middle-aged had a significantly shortened lifespan.
source: Hermaphrodites that mated within a brief (2 hr) interaction with males when young on day 3 of life (C, lime green dashed line) did not have a shortened lifespan (n.s. vs. no males) but hermaphrodites that mated within a brief period (2 hr) when middle-aged on day 7 of life (D, green dashed line) did have a significantly shortened lifespan (p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance.

claim: Young hermaphrodites were resistant to mating-induced demise if they received male sperm and seminal fluid during a brief, 2 hr interaction with males.
source: Using a different method of isolating mated hermaphrodites, we also found that young hermaphrodites (F) were resistant to mating-induced demise if they received male sperm and seminal fluid during a brief, 2 hr interaction with males (n.s. vs. no males) but that older hermaphrodites (G) were sensitive and lived shorter following a brief, 2 hr interaction with males (p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Older hermaphrodites were sensitive and lived shorter following a brief, 2 hr interaction with males.
source: Using a different method of isolating mated hermaphrodites, we also found that young hermaphrodites (F) were resistant to mating-induced demise if they received male sperm and seminal fluid during a brief, 2 hr interaction with males (n.s. vs. no males) but that older hermaphrodites (G) were sensitive and lived shorter following a brief, 2 hr interaction with males (p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G with statistical significance.

claim: Young hermaphrodites are self-fertile due to the presence of both oocytes and self-sperm.
source: Young hermaphrodites are self-fertile, due to the presence of both oocytes and self-sperm.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about C. elegans hermaphrodites.

claim: Middle-aged hermaphrodites are no longer self-fertile because they have exhausted their self-sperm.
source: In contrast, middle-aged hermaphrodites are no longer self-fertile, because they have exhausted their self-sperm, though they can still reproduce if their oocytes are fertilized by males (Riddle et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about C. elegans hermaphrodites, supported by a citation.

claim: Middle-aged hermaphrodites can still reproduce if their oocytes are fertilized by males.
source: In contrast, middle-aged hermaphrodites are no longer self-fertile, because they have exhausted their self-sperm, though they can still reproduce if their oocytes are fertilized by males (Riddle et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about C. elegans hermaphrodites, supported by a citation.

claim: Young feminized individuals (fem-1[hc17] or fog-2[q71]) were sensitive to mating-induced death and exhibited premature death and deterioration.
source: Surprisingly, young feminized individuals (fem-1[hc17] or fog-2[q71]; Doniach and Hodgkin, 1984; Schedl and Kimble, 1988) were sensitive to mating-induced death and exhibited premature death and deterioration (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, with citations for the mutant strains.

claim: Young individuals that lack self-sperm and oocytes (glp-1[e2144]) lived shorter after a brief encounter with males.
source: Consistent with the observation that the presence of self-sperm is necessary to live a normal lifespan even after a brief encounter with males, young individuals that lack self-sperm and oocytes (glp-1[e2144]; Priess et al., 1987) also lived shorter after a brief encounter with males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), even though glp-1 mutants are normally long-lived (Antebi, 2013; Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002; Hansen et al., 2013; Keith and Ghazi, 2015; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D, with citations for the mutant and its typical longevity phenotype.

claim: glp-1 mutants are normally long-lived.
source: Consistent with the observation that the presence of self-sperm is necessary to live a normal lifespan even after a brief encounter with males, young individuals that lack self-sperm and oocytes (glp-1[e2144]; Priess et al., 1987) also lived shorter after a brief encounter with males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), even though glp-1 mutants are normally long-lived (Antebi, 2013; Arantes-Oliveira et al., 2002; Hansen et al., 2013; Keith and Ghazi, 2015; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A major factor in protecting an individual from the detrimental influence of males is not youthfulness, but the presence of self-sperm.
source: Together, these results indicate that a major factor in protecting an individual from the detrimental influence of males is not youthfulness, but the presence of self-sperm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing young hermaphrodites with self-sperm to young feminized individuals without self-sperm.

claim: The first principal component separated the transcriptomes of hermaphrodites that have a shortened lifespan from those of hermaphrodites that live a normal lifespan.
source: Interestingly, the first principal component separated the transcriptomes of hermaphrodites that have a shortened lifespan (middle-aged upon mating) from those of hermaphrodites that live a normal lifespan (young upon mating, young and middle-aged without mating) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The first principal component separated the transcriptomes of feminized individuals that have a shortened lifespan from those of feminized individuals that live a normal lifespan.
source: Consistently, the first principal component also separated the transcriptomes of feminized individuals that have a shortened lifespan (young and middle-aged upon mating) from those of feminized individuals that live a normal lifespan (young and middle-aged without mating) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: GO terms linked with individuals that are resistant or sensitive to mating-induced death included translation, lipid metabolism, the innate immune response, and protein homeostasis.
source: GO terms linked with individuals that are resistant (e.g. young hermaphrodites) or sensitive to mating-induced death (e.g. young feminized) included translation, lipid metabolism, the innate immune response, and protein homeostasis (proteostasis) (Figure 2G–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, and Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), suggesting these conserved homeostatic pathways could be responsible for the lifespan differences in the response to males.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G-I and supplementary data.

claim: Translation, lipid metabolism, the innate immune response, and protein homeostasis pathways are linked with longevity.
source: Indeed, many of these pathways are linked with longevity (Kaeberlein et al., 2015; Kenyon, 2010; López-Otín et al., 2013; Riera et al., 2016; Shore and Ruvkun, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-sperm play a key role in germline quality assurance in C. elegans by triggering the clearance of carbonylated and aggregated proteins from the germline.
source: Self-sperm play a key role in germline quality assurance in C. elegans by triggering the clearance of carbonylated and aggregated proteins from the germline (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017; Goudeau and Aguilaniu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Masculinized individuals that only have self-sperm were protected from premature death induced by mating with males not only when young, but even at an older age.
source: Masculinized individuals that only have self-sperm were protected from premature death induced by mating with males not only when young, but even at an older age when hermaphrodites normally become sensitive to an encounter with males (Figure 3A–D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The presence of self-sperm is sufficient to protect from the detrimental effects on lifespan of a brief mating with males.
source: These data suggest that the presence of self-sperm is sufficient to protect from the detrimental effects on lifespan of a brief mating with males.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with masculinized individuals.

claim: Hermaphrodite mutants that are defective in self-fertilization despite maintaining self-sperm (spe-9[hc88]) were still protected from early death induced by mating with males when young.
source: Interestingly, hermaphrodite mutants that are defective in self-fertilization despite maintaining self-sperm (spe-9[hc88]; Ellis and Stanfield, 2014b; Singson et al., 1998) were still protected from early death induced by mating with males when young (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F, with citations for the mutant strain.

claim: Hermaphrodites that are defective in self-sperm maturation (due to loss of the SPE-44 transcription factor) were no longer protected from the lifespan shortening effects of mating with males when young.
source: In contrast, hermaphrodites that are defective in self-sperm maturation (due to loss of the SPE-44 transcription factor; Kasimatis et al., 2018; Kulkarni et al., 2012) were no longer protected from the lifespan shortening effects of mating with males when young (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D, with citations for the genetic manipulation.

claim: The presence of mature self-sperm, but not self-fertilization, is sufficient for the protection against mating-induced demise.
source: Thus, the presence of mature self-sperm, but not self-fertilization, is sufficient for the protection against mating-induced demise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing spe-9 and SPE-44 mutants.

claim: In C. elegans, sperm proteins are sensed by the somatic gonad and signal to the germline and somatic gonad by repressing the homeodomain transcription factor CEH-18 and the Ephrin receptor VAB-1.
source: In C. elegans, sperm proteins are known to be sensed by the somatic gonad and to signal to the germline and somatic gonad by repressing the homeodomain transcription factor CEH-18 and the Ephrin receptor VAB-1 (Figure 4A and Greenstein et al., 1994; Miller, 2001; Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The loss of CEH-18 and VAB-1 can mimic the presence of self-sperm.
source: Hence, the loss of CEH-18 and VAB-1 can mimic the presence of self-sperm (Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Deficiency in CEH-18 and VAB-1 was sufficient to protect middle-aged hermaphrodites that have depleted their self-sperm from the negative effects of mating with males.
source: Deficiency in CEH-18 and VAB-1 was sufficient to protect middle-aged hermaphrodites that have depleted their self-sperm from the negative effects of mating with males (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Deficiency in CEH-18 and VAB-1 in young feminized individuals made them resistant to brief encounter with males.
source: Interestingly, deficiency in CEH-18 and VAB-1 in young feminized individuals made them resistant to brief encounter with males (Figure 4B,C), indicating that this conserved pathway could be sufficient to protect females against the negative impact of males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The CEH-18/VAB-1 pathway is sufficient to protect females against the negative impact of males.
source: Interestingly, deficiency in CEH-18 and VAB-1 in young feminized individuals made them resistant to brief encounter with males (Figure 4B,C), indicating that this conserved pathway could be sufficient to protect females against the negative impact of males.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with feminized individuals lacking CEH-18 and VAB-1.

claim: Several genes that interact genetically or physically with CEH-18, including the chromatin modifiers set-33 and jmjd-3.2, were differentially expressed between young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals that have successfully mated with males.
source: In contrast, several genes that interact genetically or physically with CEH-18, including the chromatin modifiers set-33 and jmjd-3.2, were differentially expressed between young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals that have successfully mated with males (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and network analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Differences in chromatin state between young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals may contribute to the transcriptional effect of the CEH-18 sperm-sensing transcription factor in the resistance and sensitivity to mating-induced death.
source: These observations suggest that differences in chromatin state between young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals may contribute to the transcriptional effect of the CEH-18 sperm-sensing transcription factor in the resistance and sensitivity to mating-induced death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential expression of chromatin modifiers.

claim: The sperm-sensing transcription factor CEH-18 may directly regulate genes that affect longevity.
source: Interestingly, GO term enrichment of these genes revealed several terms linked with longevity, including 'Determination of adult lifespan' (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the sperm-sensing transcription factor CEH-18 may directly regulate genes that affect longevity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Self-sperm protect individuals from mating-induced death by repressing a sperm-sensing pathway in the somatic gonad.
source: Together, these results show that self-sperm protect individuals, even older ones, from mating-induced death by repressing a sperm-sensing pathway in the somatic gonad, which could in turn protect hermaphrodites by altering chromatin and transcriptional networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on the CEH-18/VAB-1 pathway and transcriptional analysis.

claim: The C. elegans ancestor was a gonochoric species with true females and obligatory males.
source: The C. elegans ancestor was a gonochoric species with true females and obligatory males (Kiontke et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hermaphroditism evolved at least three times independently in the Caenorhabditis lineage (in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis).
source: Hermaphroditism evolved at least three times independently in this lineage (in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis) (Ellis and Lin, 2014a; Guo et al., 2009; Hill et al., 2006; Kiontke et al., 2004; Kiontke et al., 2011; Nayak et al., 2005; Thomas et al., 2012) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: C. remanei and C. brenneri remained true females.
source: Other nematode species remained true females (e.g. C. remanei and C. brenneri) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: C. brenneri females lived a normal lifespan if they mated with a male during brief, two-hour interaction when young or middle-aged.
source: We found that C. remanei and C. brenneri females lived normal lifespans following brief, two-hour interactions with males at all of the ages we tested (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the differential sensitivity of old versus young hermaphrodites may have evolved in hermaphroditic species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: C. remanei females lived normal lifespans following brief, two-hour interactions with males at all of the ages tested.
source: We found that C. remanei and C. brenneri females lived normal lifespans following brief, two-hour interactions with males at all of the ages we tested (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the differential sensitivity of old versus young hermaphrodites may have evolved in hermaphroditic species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The differential sensitivity of old versus young hermaphrodites may have evolved in hermaphroditic species.
source: We found that C. remanei and C. brenneri females lived normal lifespans following brief, two-hour interactions with males at all of the ages we tested (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the differential sensitivity of old versus young hermaphrodites may have evolved in hermaphroditic species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the comparison of hermaphroditic and female species.

claim: Young C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have self-sperm) resisted a brief exposure to males and lived a normal lifespan.
source: Indeed, we found that young C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have self-sperm) resisted a brief exposure to males and lived a normal lifespan whereas middle-aged C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have depleted their self-sperm) succumbed to brief encounter with males (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Middle-aged C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have depleted their self-sperm) succumbed to brief encounter with males.
source: Indeed, we found that young C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have self-sperm) resisted a brief exposure to males and lived a normal lifespan whereas middle-aged C. briggsae hermaphrodites (which have depleted their self-sperm) succumbed to brief encounter with males (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Feminized individuals in C. briggsae became sensitive to a brief interaction with males when young and exhibited premature death.
source: Interestingly, feminized individuals in C. briggsae (due to a different mutation than C. elegans, the she-1 feminizing mutation, which affects sex determination; Guo et al., 2009), also became sensitive to a brief interaction with males when young and exhibited premature death (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, with a citation for the mutation.

claim: Knock-down of the C. briggsae sperm-sensing genes protected middle-aged hermaphrodites (which are self-sperm depleted) from the lifespan shortening effects of a brief interaction with males.
source: Interestingly, knock-down of the C. briggsae sperm-sensing genes protected middle-aged hermaphrodites (which are self-sperm depleted) from the lifespan shortening effects of a brief interaction with males (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Hermaphroditism, notably the presence of self-sperm and detection by the sperm-sensing pathway, may have co-evolved more than once with strategies to protect from the detrimental effect of sexual interactions with the opposite sex.
source: Together, these results suggest that hermaphroditism, notably the presence of self-sperm and detection by the sperm-sensing pathway, may have co-evolved more than once with strategies to protect from the detrimental effect of sexual interactions with the opposite sex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of the protective mechanism in C. elegans and C. briggsae.

claim: Male sperm out-compete hermaphroditic self-sperm.
source: As male sperm out-compete hermaphroditic self-sperm (LaMunyon and Samuel, 1999; Ward and Carrel, 1979), such a strategy would also allow for the hermaphroditic self-sperm to be used.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The sperm-sensing pathway is conserved in species with true females and is sufficient to protect feminized individuals.
source: Because the sperm-sensing pathway is conserved in species with true females and is sufficient to protect feminized individuals, this pathway could be leveraged to protect the soma in a conserved manner, even in other species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of the pathway and its sufficiency in feminized individuals.

claim: The presence of self-sperm in hermaphrodites decreases attraction of and mating with males.
source: The presence of self-sperm in hermaphrodites is also known to decrease attraction of and mating with males (Garcia et al., 2007; Leighton et al., 2014; Morsci et al., 2011; Shi and Murphy, 2014), and we did account for this in our study by selecting only mated individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-sperm may be evolutionary important to ensure that hermaphrodites produce as many of their own self-progeny as possible before succumbing to mating-induced death.
source: Hence, self-sperm may be evolutionary important to ensure, in several different ways, that hermaphrodites produce as many of their own self-progeny as possible before succumbing to mating-induced death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the multiple roles of self-sperm.

claim: The protective effect of self-sperm on the soma appears to have evolved independently in two distantly-related species.
source: However, the protective effect of self-sperm on the soma appears to have evolved independently in two distantly-related species, suggesting that it is important for nematode hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in C. elegans and C. briggsae.

claim: The role of self-sperm as a signal to regulate the response to the opposite sex may have evolved in other animals, including self-fertilizing hermaphroditic species.
source: The role of self-sperm as a signal to regulate the response to the opposite sex may also have evolved in other animals, including self-fertilizing hermaphroditic species (e.g. snails, slugs, and the vertebrate mangrove killifish) (Jarne and Auld, 2006; Mackiewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to examples of other hermaphroditic species.

claim: The ancestor of C. elegans and related nematodes did not have self-sperm-mediated protection from mating-induced death.
source: The ancestor of C. elegans and related nematodes did not have self-sperm-mediated protection from mating-induced death and our data indicate that self-sperm mediated protection was an evolutionary innovation in the C. elegans and C. briggsae lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: Self-sperm mediated protection was an evolutionary innovation in the C. elegans and C. briggsae lineages.
source: The ancestor of C. elegans and related nematodes did not have self-sperm-mediated protection from mating-induced death and our data indicate that self-sperm mediated protection was an evolutionary innovation in the C. elegans and C. briggsae lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: The most parsimonious model is that the hermaphroditic lineages linked ancestral protection mechanisms with self-sperm.
source: However, given that self-sperm mediated mating-induced death protection evolved more than once in Caenorhabditis nematodes, the most parsimonious model is that the hermaphroditic lineages linked ancestral protection mechanisms with self-sperm.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the independent evolution of the mechanism.

claim: The signaling pathways that are engaged by self-sperm (an Ephrin receptor and homeodomain transcription factor) are conserved in nematodes.
source: Indeed, the signaling pathways that are engaged by self-sperm (an Ephrin receptor and homeodomain transcription factor) are conserved in nematodes, suggesting that these ancestral pathways were harnessed in unique ways in the hermaphroditic lineages to evolve self-sperm mediated resistance to mating-induced death.
evidence: This is a statement based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ancestral pathways were harnessed in unique ways in the hermaphroditic lineages to evolve self-sperm mediated resistance to mating-induced death.
source: Indeed, the signaling pathways that are engaged by self-sperm (an Ephrin receptor and homeodomain transcription factor) are conserved in nematodes, suggesting that these ancestral pathways were harnessed in unique ways in the hermaphroditic lineages to evolve self-sperm mediated resistance to mating-induced death.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of the pathways.

claim: Protective mechanisms could be 'tuned up' in female species by mimicking activation of the signaling pathways that are triggered by self-sperm.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that such protective mechanisms could also be 'tuned up' in female species by mimicking activation of the signaling pathways that are triggered by self-sperm.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the sufficiency of the pathway in feminized individuals.

claim: The Ephrin receptor that detects the presence of sperm is conserved in mammals.
source: Interestingly, the Ephrin receptor that detects the presence of sperm is conserved in mammals, it is expressed in the somatic gonad (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; Uhlén et al., 2015), and is linked with mammalian fertility (Barban et al., 2016; Buensuceso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Ephrin receptor is expressed in the somatic gonad in mammals.
source: Interestingly, the Ephrin receptor that detects the presence of sperm is conserved in mammals, it is expressed in the somatic gonad (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; Uhlén et al., 2015), and is linked with mammalian fertility (Barban et al., 2016; Buensuceso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Ephrin receptor is linked with mammalian fertility.
source: Interestingly, the Ephrin receptor that detects the presence of sperm is conserved in mammals, it is expressed in the somatic gonad (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; Uhlén et al., 2015), and is linked with mammalian fertility (Barban et al., 2016; Buensuceso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some of the mechanisms that signal between germline and soma could be used more generally to protect against the negative impact of sexual interactions in other species.
source: Thus, some of the mechanisms that signal between germline and soma could be used more generally to protect against the negative impact of sexual interactions in other species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of the Ephrin receptor.

claim: Fertilization has a rejuvenating effect in the germline and resets the aging clock in each generation.
source: Fertilization has a rejuvenating effect in the germline and resets the aging clock in each generation (Rando and Chang, 2012; Unal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-sperm can clear carbonylated and aggregated proteins, two aging hallmarks, in the germline of C. elegans.
source: Consistently, self-sperm can clear carbonylated and aggregated proteins, two aging hallmarks, in the germline of C. elegans (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017; Goudeau and Aguilaniu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Resetting of aging features can be achieved to some degree in mammalian somatic cells by the process of reprogramming to induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Resetting of aging features can be achieved to some degree in mammalian somatic cells by the process of reprogramming to induced pluripotent stem cells, which can mimic fertilization and has a 'rejuvenating' capacity (Rando and Chang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Triggering rejuvenating factors in somatic cells, in a manner that is uncoupled from de-differentiation, has been recently suggested to be a potential rejuvenation strategy.
source: In mammals, triggering rejuvenating factors in somatic cells, in a manner that is uncoupled from de-differentiation, has been recently suggested to be a potential rejuvenation strategy (Ocampo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is possible that the protective properties of self-sperm, or even sperm itself, are conserved in other species, including mammals.
source: Given the effect of sperm and fertilization on resetting the aging clock in the germline, as well as the conservation of key elements of the sensing pathway, it is possible that the protective properties of self-sperm, or even sperm itself, are conserved in other species, including mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of pathways and the rejuvenating effects of sperm.

claim: These findings could open new strategies for harnessing the potential of gametes and their sensing pathways to 'reset' some hallmarks of aging.
source: These findings could open new strategies for harnessing the potential of gametes and their sensing pathways to 'reset' some hallmarks of aging.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: The continuous presence of young males beginning at the onset of adulthood shortens hermaphrodite lifespan.
source: The continuous presence of young males beginning at the onset of adulthood (day 3 of life) shortens hermaphrodite lifespan (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: Young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals do not have different levels of multiple mating during a two-hour period.
source: Young hermaphrodites and feminized individuals do not have different levels of multiple mating during a two-hour period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Young and middle-aged hermaphrodites do not have different sensitivities to 24 hr of exposure to 5 ng/mL MitoTracker Red CMXRos in OP50-1 bacteria.
source: Young and middle-aged hermaphrodites (E) and feminized worms (fem-1[hc17], F) do not have different sensitivities to 24 hr of exposure to 5 ng/mL MitoTracker Red CMXRos in OP50-1 bacteria (p=0.0091 for E and n.s. for F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F with statistical analysis.

claim: Receiving male sperm when young or middle-aged reduced the lifespan of feminized (fog-2[q71]) individuals.
source: Receiving male sperm (dashed lines) when young (day 3 of life) or middle-aged (day 7 of life) reduced the lifespan of feminized (fog-2[q71]) individuals (p<0.0001 for both young and middle-aged).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B with statistical significance.

claim: Receiving male sperm when young or middle-aged shortened the lifespan of sterile (glp-1[e2144]) individuals.
source: Receiving male sperm (dashed lines) when young (C, day 3 of life) or middle-aged (D, day 6 of life) shortened the lifespan of sterile (glp-1[e2144]) individuals (p=0.0004 and p=0.0003, young and middle-aged, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D with statistical significance.

claim: Both hermaphrodites and masculinized individuals were susceptible to long-term male-induced demise and lived shorter when young males were present throughout all of adulthood.
source: However, both hermaphrodites and masculinized individuals were susceptible to long-term male-induced demise and lived shorter when young males were present throughout all of adulthood (dotted lines, p<0.0001 vs. no males for A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B with statistical significance.

claim: Young hermaphrodites that have defective self-sperm due to the absence of the SPE-44 transcription factor are not fully protected from a brief, 2 hr interaction with males.
source: Young hermaphrodites that have defective self-sperm due to the absence of the SPE-44 transcription factor (panel D, fxIs1[pie-1p::TIR1::mRuby]; spe-44(fx110[spe-44::degron]) grown on 1 mM auxin), are not fully protected from a brief, 2 hr interaction with males (p=0.0303 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D with statistical significance.

claim: The same strain cultured without auxin and thus with normal levels of SPE-44 and normal sperm lives a normal lifespan after a brief 2 hr interaction with males.
source: The same strain cultured without auxin and thus with normal levels of SPE-44 and normal sperm (panel C) lives a normal lifespan after a brief 2 hr interaction with males (n.s. vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: C. brenneri female lifespan was shortened if they interacted with males for a longer period of time.
source: C.brenneri female lifespan was shortened if they interacted with males for a longer period of time. Interacting with males for their entire lifetime significantly shortened lifespan (orange dashed line, p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: C. brenneri female lifespan was reduced when interacting with males for one day when young.
source: C. brenneri female lifespan was also reduced when interacting with males for one day when young (blue dashed line, p=0.0011 vs. no males) or for three days when young (pink dashed line, p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: C. remanei females lived a normal lifespan after a brief, 2 hr mating with males at all the ages tested but succumbed when they interacted with young males for their entire lifetime.
source: C. remanei females lived a normal lifespan after a brief, 2 hr mating with males at all the ages tested (n.s. vs. no males) but succumbed when they interacted with young males for their entire lifetime (p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: The wild-type C. briggsae strain AF16 was more resistant to a brief interaction with males when young compared to when middle-aged.
source: The wild-type C. briggsae strain AF16 was more resistant to a brief interaction with males when young (day 3 or 4 of life, p=0.0093 vs. no males and p<0.0001 vs. middle-aged interaction) compared to when middle-aged (day 7 or 8 of life, p<0.0001 vs. no males).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C with statistical significance.
